units.2 Maccabees 2:19: The events concerning Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, the purification of the greatest temple and the dedication of the altar,
units.2 Maccabees 2:20: and also the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator,
units.2 Maccabees 2:21: and the manifestations from heaven to those who zealously performed brave deeds for Judaism, so that, although few, they plundered the whole land and pursued the barbarian multitudes,

units.2 Maccabees 2:23: these things, set forth by Jason of Cyrene in five books, we shall attempt to abridge into one composition.
units.2 Maccabees 2:24: For, seeing the abundance of figures and the difficulty caused by the mass of material for those who wish to enter into the narratives of the history,
units.2 Maccabees 2:25: we have taken thought for the pleasure of those who wish to read, for the ease of those eager to commit it to memory, and for the benefit of everyone who encounters it.
units.2 Maccabees 2:27: Just as it is not easy for someone preparing a banquet and seeking others’ benefit, nevertheless, for the gratitude of the many, we will gladly bear the hard work.
units.2 Maccabees 2:28: We leave the precise treatment of each matter to the historian, while labouring to follow the outlines of the abridgement.
units.2 Maccabees 2:30: To enter deeply into matters, range widely in the discussion, and investigate the particulars belongs to the original historian.
units.2 Maccabees 2:31: But the person making a recasting should be permitted to pursue concise expression and set aside an exhaustive treatment of the subject.
units.2 Maccabees 2:32: Let us therefore begin the narrative here, adding only this much to what has already been said: it would be foolish to expand the preface to the history while abridging the history itself.

units.2 Maccabees 3:1: While the holy city was inhabited in complete peace and the laws were being kept most carefully because of the high priest Onias’s piety and hatred of wickedness,
units.2 Maccabees 3:2: even the kings themselves honoured the place and glorified the temple with their finest gifts,
units.2 Maccabees 3:3: so that Seleucus, king of Asia, also supplied from his own revenues all the expenses required for the service of the sacrifices.
units.2 Maccabees 3:4: But a certain Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin, who had been appointed overseer of the temple, disagreed with the high priest over the administration of the city’s market.
units.2 Maccabees 3:5: Unable to overcome Onias, he went to Apollonius son of Thraseas, who at that time was governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.
units.2 Maccabees 3:6: He reported that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of indescribable riches, so that the amount of money was beyond counting, and that it did not belong to the account for the sacrifices; these funds, he said, could fall under the king’s authority.
units.2 Maccabees 3:7: Apollonius met the king and informed him about the money reported to him. The king chose Heliodorus, his chief minister, and sent him with orders to remove that money.
units.2 Maccabees 3:8: Heliodorus immediately began his journey, ostensibly to inspect the cities of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, but actually to carry out the king’s intention.
units.2 Maccabees 3:9: When he arrived in Jerusalem and was cordially received by the city’s high priest, he related the information that had been given and explained why he was there. He asked whether these things were really so.
units.2 Maccabees 3:10: The high priest explained that they were deposits belonging to widows and orphans,
units.2 Maccabees 3:11: and that some also belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man of very high standing. Thus the impious Simon had misrepresented matters. In all there were four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold.
units.2 Maccabees 3:12: It was utterly impossible, he said, that those who had trusted in the holiness of the place and in the dignity and inviolability of the temple honoured throughout the whole world should suffer injustice.
units.2 Maccabees 3:13: But Heliodorus, because of his royal instructions, insisted that the money must certainly be taken into the royal treasury.
units.2 Maccabees 3:14: He appointed a day and went in to arrange the inspection of these things. There was no small anguish throughout the city.
units.2 Maccabees 3:15: The priests threw themselves down before the altar in their priestly robes, calling to heaven upon the One who had legislated about deposits, that He would keep them safe for those who had entrusted them.
units.2 Maccabees 3:19: Women, girded with sackcloth beneath their breasts, thronged the streets. Of the secluded virgins, some ran together to the gateways, some to the walls, and others leaned out through the windows.
units.2 Maccabees 3:20: All of them stretched their hands toward heaven and offered their entreaty.
units.2 Maccabees 3:21: It was pitiful to see the mingled multitude falling prostrate, and the high priest waiting in great anguish.
units.2 Maccabees 3:22: So they called on the all-powerful Lord to keep the entrusted property safe and fully secure for those who had entrusted it.

units.Jonah 2:1: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.

units.2 Maccabees 4:7: When Seleucus departed this life and Antiochus, called Epiphanes, took over the kingdom, Jason, Onias’s brother, obtained the high priesthood by fraud.
units.2 Maccabees 4:8: In an audience he promised the king three hundred sixty talents of silver, and eighty talents from another source of revenue.
units.2 Maccabees 4:9: Beyond these he promised to pay a further one hundred fifty if he were permitted by royal authority to establish a gymnasium and a training institution for young men, and to enroll the people in Jerusalem as Antiochenes.
units.2 Maccabees 4:10: When the king consented and Jason gained office, he immediately turned his fellow countrymen toward the Greek manner of life.
units.2 Maccabees 4:11: He set aside the benevolent royal concessions established for the Jews through John, the father of Eupolemus, who had undertaken the embassy to the Romans for friendship and alliance. Abolishing the lawful forms of civic life, he introduced unlawful customs.
units.2 Maccabees 4:12: For he eagerly established a gymnasium immediately beneath the citadel and brought the most distinguished young men under his direction to wear the broad-brimmed hat.
units.2 Maccabees 4:13: There was such an upsurge of Hellenism and advance of foreign ways because of the surpassing impurity of the impious Jason, who was no high priest,
units.2 Maccabees 4:15: They regarded their ancestral honours as nothing and considered Greek distinctions the finest.
units.2 Maccabees 4:16: For this reason a difficult crisis overtook them: those whose ways they admired and whom they wished to resemble in everything became their enemies and punishers.
units.2 Maccabees 4:17: For acting impiously against the divine laws is no light matter; the ensuing time will show this.
units.Malachi 1:6: “A son honors his father, and a slave his master. If I am a father, where is My honor? If I am a master, where is the fear of Me?” says the Lord Almighty. You priests who belittle My name! But you said, “How have we belittled Thy name?”
units.Malachi 1:7: “By bringing polluted loaves to My altar.” But you said, “How have we polluted them?” “By your saying, ‘The Lord’s table is despised, and the foods placed upon it are despised.’”
units.Malachi 1:8: “For if you bring a blind animal for sacrifice, is that not evil? If you bring one that is lame or sick, is that not evil? Bring it, then, to your ruler! Will he accept it? Will he show you favor?” says the Lord Almighty.
units.Malachi 1:9: “And now appease the face of your God and plead with Him. These things have happened in your hands. Will I show favor to any of you?” says the Lord Almighty.
units.Malachi 1:10: “For even among you doors will be shut, and you will not kindle My altar for nothing. I have no desire for you,” says the Lord Almighty, “and I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands.”

reread_versions.relationship: Thematic comparison of divine protection of the holy city
reread_versions.rationale: The letter credits God with driving out opponents arrayed against the holy city. The psalm describes God supporting His city while assembled kings are troubled and shaken. Both locate the city's security in God's action against threatening rulers; the psalm is not identified as a prediction or account of this particular expulsion.
reread_versions.source_text: for He Himself drove out those arrayed against us in the holy city.

reread_versions.relationship: Liturgical parallel of a leader and answering assembly
reread_versions.rationale: Jonathan begins the prayer while the priests and others respond during the sacrifice; Esdras blesses the Lord and all the people answer Amen. Both depict public prayer with a leader and a responding congregation. The names, occasions and words of response remain distinct, and Jonathan is not identified with Esdras.
reread_versions.source_text: While the sacrifice was being consumed, the priests offered prayer—the priests and everyone—with Jonathan beginning and the others responding, as Nehemiah did.

target_units.text: Esdras blessed the Lord, the great God. All the people answered and said, “Amen,” lifting their hands, and they bowed and worshiped the Lord with their faces to the ground.

reread_versions.rationale: The priests sing hymns in response after the sacrificial prayer; at the foundation of the Lord's house, priests and Levites participate in answering praise and thanksgiving. The shared practice is responsive temple praise, without identifying the unnamed hymns in Maccabees as Ezra's quoted refrain or equating the ceremonies.
reread_versions.source_text: The priests sang the hymns in response.

target_units.text: They laid the foundation for building the Lord’s house, and the priests stood in their vestments with trumpets, and the Levites, sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the Lord according to the directions of David king of Israel.

They answered in praise and thanksgiving to the Lord: “For it is good, for His mercy toward Israel endures for ever.” All the people sounded a great cry of praise to the Lord at the founding of the Lord’s house.

reread_versions.relationship: Archival preservation of royal provisions for sacred gifts
reread_versions.rationale: Nehemiah's reported library includes kings' letters about dedicated gifts. Ezra describes a treasury-library search and a preserved memorandum of Cyrus's provisions for rebuilding the Jerusalem house and returning its gold and silver vessels. Both associate collected written royal records with sacred endowments; Ezra's memorandum is not asserted to be one of Nehemiah's particular letters or in the same archive.
reread_versions.source_text: These same things were related in the records and in the memoirs concerning Nehemiah, and also how, in establishing a library, he gathered together the books concerning the kings and prophets, the writings of David, and kings’ letters concerning dedicated gifts.

target_units.text: Then Darius the king issued a decision and made a search in the libraries where the treasury is kept in Babylon.
A scroll was found in a city, in the citadel of the city of the Medes, and this was written in it: “Memorandum:

In the first year of Cyrus the king, King Cyrus issued a decision concerning the house of God in Jerusalem: Let the house be built, and the place where they sacrifice the sacrifices. He set an elevation: sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide,
with three courses of strong stone and one wooden course. The expense will be paid from the king’s house.

And let the silver and gold vessels of God’s house, which Nabouchodonosor took from the house in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon, be given back and go to the sanctuary in Jerusalem, to the place where they were set in God’s house.”

reread_versions.relationship: Literary reflection on the bodily cost of study and writing
reread_versions.rationale: The abridger describes the work of producing the condensed history as sweat and sleeplessness. Ecclesiastes links the making of many books and much study with weariness of the flesh. Both explicitly connect literary work with bodily strain, while the abridger willingly undertakes the task and Ecclesiastes issues a caution.
reread_versions.source_text: For us who have undertaken the hard work of abridgement, the task is not easy; it involves sweat and sleeplessness.

target_units.text: My son, beware of making many books; there is no limit, and much study is weariness of the flesh.

reread_versions.relationship: Comparison of building metaphors for different responsibilities
reread_versions.rationale: The abridger distinguishes an architect's concern for the whole foundation from the decorator's work to explain historian and abridger roles. Paul distinguishes laying a foundation as a master builder from another person's building upon it. Both use construction roles to distinguish responsibilities; Paul's foundation is explicitly Jesus Christ, and the literary historian is not equated with that foundation.
reread_versions.source_text: For just as the architect of a new house must consider its whole foundation, while the person undertaking its encaustic work and painting must examine what is suitable for decoration, so, I think, it is with us.

target_units.text: According to the grace of God given to me, I laid a foundation as a wise master builder, and another builds upon it. But let each one watch how he builds upon it.

reread_versions.relationship: Visible facial distress revealing inner sorrow
reread_versions.rationale: Onias's changed face reveals the anguish of his soul to observers. The king reads the speaker's distressed face as distress of heart, and the speaker explains his grief over the devastated city. Both make facial appearance an outward sign of inward sorrow; the threatened temple deposits and the burned city gates are different causes.
reread_versions.source_text: Whoever saw the high priest’s appearance was wounded in mind, for his face and altered complexion revealed his soul’s anguish.

target_units.text: The king said to me, “Why is your face distressed when you are not unwell? This is nothing but distress of heart.” I became very greatly afraid.

reread_versions.rationale: People leave their houses for public supplication because the sanctuary is threatened with contempt, while the priests plead in the surrounding scene. Joel calls the congregation together and has the priests ask that God's inheritance not be given to reproach or foreign rule. Both present communal assembly and priestly petition against disgrace, without treating Heliodorus's mission as the fulfilment of Joel's summons.
reread_versions.source_text: People also rushed out of their houses in crowds for a public supplication, because the place was about to be treated with contempt.

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Consecrate a fast; proclaim a service.
Gather the people; consecrate the congregation. Choose elders; gather infants nursing at breasts. Let the bridegroom leave his bedroom and the bride her bridal chamber.

In the midst of the altar’s platform the priests who minister to the Lord will weep and say, “Spare Thy people, Lord, and do not give Thine inheritance to reproach, for nations to rule over them, so that they do not say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”

reread_versions.relationship: Sacrifice and vows in response to preserved life
reread_versions.rationale: Heliodorus sacrifices and makes vows to the One who preserved his life after his near-fatal ordeal. Jonah recalls his failing life and promises thankful sacrifice and repayment of his vows while praying for deliverance. Both connect endangered life, appeal to the Lord, sacrifice and vows; Heliodorus's enacted offering and Jonah's promised offering remain distinct.
reread_versions.source_text: Heliodorus offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made very great vows to the One who had preserved his life. He warmly took leave of Onias and departed with his company to the king.

target_units.text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.

But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”

reread_versions.rationale: The priests in Maccabees despise the temple and neglect its sacrifices in favour of athletic exercises. Malachi rebukes priests who belittle God's name and treat His table as despised by bringing polluted and defective offerings. Both condemn priests' contempt for their altar responsibilities, with neglect for athletics distinguished from the presentation of unacceptable offerings.
reread_versions.source_text: that the priests were no longer eager for the services of the altar. Despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried to take part in the unlawful provision of exercises in the wrestling ground after the signal for the discus.

reread_versions.relationship: Royal mourning for a man unjustly killed
reread_versions.rationale: Antiochus weeps over Onias after learning of his unjust murder and admiring his conduct. David leads mourning for Abner, weeps at his grave and laments his fall before men of injustice. Both narratives show a king grieving an unjust killing, without equating the victims, their offices or the kings' later treatment of the killers.
reread_versions.source_text: Antiochus was deeply grieved, moved to pity, and wept because of the deceased man’s self-restraint and admirable conduct.

target_units.text: David said to Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your garments, put on sackcloth, and beat yourselves in mourning before Abner.” King David walked behind the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king lifted his voice and wept at his grave, and all the people wept over Abner.
The king lamented over Abner and said, “Should Abner die according to Nabal’s death?
Your hands were not bound; your feet were not in fetters. He did not bring near, as Nabal; before men of injustice you fell.” All the people gathered to weep over him.

reread_versions.relationship: Loss of mourning and honourable burial
reread_versions.rationale: Jason, who left others unburied, receives neither mourning nor funeral care or an ancestral tomb. Jeremiah announces that Jehoiakim will not be mourned and will receive a dishonourable burial outside Jerusalem's gate. Both portray deprivation of mourning and proper burial as an ignominious end, without identifying Jason with Jehoiakim or assigning the same disposal of the body to both.
reread_versions.source_text: He who had thrown out multitudes unburied went unmourned and received neither any funeral care whatever nor a place in his ancestral tomb.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah: Woe upon this man! They will certainly not mourn him, O brother! Nor will they weep for him, Alas, lord!
He will be buried with a donkey’s burial; swept up, he will be thrown beyond Jerusalem’s gate.

reread_versions.relationship: Comparison of lists describing slaughter across age and sex
reread_versions.rationale: The massacre narrative lists young and old, women, children, virgins and infants among those killed. Ezekiel's vision similarly lists old men, young men, maidens, infants and women in the order to strike Jerusalem. The shared enumeration conveys the breadth of the killing; the vision explicitly exempts those bearing the sign, and Antiochus's soldiers are not identified with its agents or granted its divine commission.
reread_versions.source_text: There was killing of young and old, destruction of boys, women and children, and slaughter of virgins and infants.

target_units.text: To these others He said while I listened, “Go behind him into the city and strike. Do not spare with your eyes, and have no mercy.

Old man, young man, maiden, infants and women—kill them to obliteration. But do not approach anyone upon whom the sign is. Begin at My holy places.” They began with the elderly men who were inside the house.

reread_versions.relationship: Wisdom principle linking honourable age and righteousness
reread_versions.rationale: Eleazar judges his resolve by the dignity of old age and his lifelong excellent conduct, with God's law foremost. Proverbs calls old age a crown of boasting found in ways of righteousness. The narrative embodies the connection between honourable age and righteous conduct; the proverb does not name Eleazar or prescribe his particular martyrdom.
reread_versions.source_text: But he adopted a noble resolve, worthy of his age, the dignity of his old age, his acquired and distinguished gray hair, his excellent conduct from childhood, and still more the holy legislation established by God. Accordingly he declared at once that they should send him to Hades.

target_units.text: Old age is a crown of boasting, and it is found in ways of righteousness.

reread_versions.relationship: Wisdom principle of conduct fitting gray hair
reread_versions.rationale: Eleazar's resolve is described as worthy of his age and distinguished gray hair, acquired through a life of excellent conduct. Sirach calls judgment, wisdom and counsel fitting for gray hair and elders, and names fear of the Lord their boast. Both link the honour of age to moral and discerning conduct, without claiming Sirach describes Eleazar's biography or commands his particular decision.

target_units.text: How fitting is judgment for gray hair, and knowledge of counsel for elders!
How fitting is wisdom for the old, and thought and counsel for the honored!
Long experience is the crown of the old, and their boast is the fear of the Lord.

reread_versions.relationship: Liturgical parallel of a leader and answering assembly
reread_versions.rationale: Jonathan begins the prayer while the priests and others respond during the sacrifice; Esdras blesses the Lord and all the people answer Amen. Both depict public prayer with a leader and a responding congregation. The occasions remain distinct; Maccabees does not specify an Amen response, and Jonathan is not identified with Esdras.
reread_versions.source_text: While the sacrifice was being consumed, the priests offered prayer—the priests and everyone—with Jonathan beginning and the others responding, as Nehemiah did.

target_units.text: Esdras blessed the Lord, the great God. All the people answered and said, “Amen,” lifting their hands, and they bowed and worshiped the Lord with their faces to the ground.

reread_versions.relationship: Comparison of building metaphors for different responsibilities
reread_versions.rationale: The abridger distinguishes an architect's concern for the whole foundation from the decorator's work to explain historian and abridger roles. Paul distinguishes laying a foundation as a master builder from another person's building upon it. Both use construction roles to distinguish responsibilities; Paul's foundation is explicitly Jesus Christ, and the literary historian is not equated with that foundation.
reread_versions.source_text: For just as the architect of a new house must consider its whole foundation, while the person undertaking its encaustic work and painting must examine what is suitable for decoration, so, I think, it is with us.

target_units.text: According to the grace of God given to me, I laid a foundation as a wise master builder, and another builds upon it. But let each one watch how he builds upon it.
For no one can lay another foundation besides the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

reread_versions.relationship: Sacrifice and vows after danger to life
reread_versions.rationale: Heliodorus sacrifices and makes vows to the One who preserved his life after his near-fatal ordeal. Jonah recalls his failing life and promises thankful sacrifice and repayment of his vows while praying for deliverance. Both connect endangered life, appeal to the Lord, sacrifice and vows; Heliodorus's enacted offering and Jonah's promised offering remain distinct.
reread_versions.source_text: Heliodorus offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made very great vows to the One who had preserved his life. He warmly took leave of Onias and departed with his company to the king.

target_units.text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.
Those who guard vain and false things abandoned their mercy.
But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”

case.source_text: Dread and bodily shuddering had come over the man, making the pain lodged in his heart plain to those who looked at him.
case.reason: The shared bodily trembling does not establish a sufficiently particular relationship: Onias visibly shudders over the threatened deposits, while Habakkuk describes bodily terror at the sound of the prayer of his lips. No shared event or distinctive action beyond distress was verified.

case.source_text: The king himself and those with him were astonished at the young man’s spirit, for he regarded his pains as nothing.
case.reason: Both authorities are amazed, but the young man is admired for disregarding bodily pains, whereas the council marvels at the boldness of unlettered Peter and John. The read Acts context describes threats and release, not the torture or bodily endurance that is the focus here; this broad reaction is not retained as a distinct match.

target_units.text: I kept watch, and my belly was terrified at the sound of the prayer of my lips. Trembling entered my bones, and my bodily condition beneath me was troubled. I will rest on a day of affliction, to go up to the people of my sojourning.

target_units.text: When they observed Peter’s and John’s boldness and realized that they were unlettered, ordinary men, they were amazed. They also recognized that they had been with Jesus.
Seeing the man who had been healed standing with them, they had nothing to say against it.
They ordered them to leave the council and conferred with one another,
saying, “What should we do with these men? That a notable sign has taken place through them is evident to everyone living in Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it.
But so that it spreads no further among the people, let us warn them with threats not to speak to anyone in this name again.”
They called them in and ordered them neither to speak nor to teach at all in the name of Jesus.
Peter and John answered them, “Judge whether it is right before God to listen to you rather than to God;
for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
After further threats, they released them, finding no way to punish them because of the people, since everyone was glorifying God for what had happened.
